study_characteristics.study_objective: To dissect heterogeneous neurodevelopmental deviations of the affective brain circuitry in disruptive behavior disorders (DBD) using normative modeling of functional (emotion matching task) and anatomical MRI data, and to integrate these deviations across modalities using linked independent component analysis to explain aggressive behavior at a symptom level.

deviation_metric.answer: Subject-specific Z-scores (normative probability maps, NPMs) quantifying voxel-wise deviations from the normative model. NPMs were thresholded at Z = ±2.6 (p < 0.005) for comparison across participants. Total number of positive and negative deviations extracted per subject. Unthresholded Z-transformed deviation maps used for linked ICA integration.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Statistical methods: (1) Mann-Whitney U tests to compare total deviation counts between DBD cases and controls, with FDR correction using Benjamini-Hochberg method. (2) PALM (Permutation Analysis of Linear Models) for threshold-free cluster-enhanced group differences on normative deviation maps, family-wise error corrected. (3) Linked ICA to integrate unthresholded deviation maps across four modalities (negative faces, positive/neutral faces, shapes, anatomy) estimating 20 independent components. (4) Logistic regression using all 20 component loadings to predict DBD diagnosis (χ²=39.2, df=20, p=0.006; McFadden's R²=23%). (5) Spearman correlations between component loadings and aggression factor (derived from PCA with VARIMAX rotation on CBCL conduct/oppositional, ICU total, RPQ reactive/proactive), with FDR correction. (6) Mann-Whitney U tests for component differences between cases and controls. (7) Nonparametric partial correlations controlling for IQ, medication, pubertal status, internalizing symptoms, and ADHD symptoms.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: DBD cases showed increased positive age-related deviations in the amygdala and face-processing network; multimodal integration via linked ICA explained 23% of variance in DBD phenotype, with component 8 (DMN, striatum, amygdala) negatively associated with aggression across the whole sample.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Normative modeling revealed that DBD cases exhibited significantly more positive deviations (higher age-related activity) than controls across all functional measures (negative faces, positive/neutral faces, shapes; all pFDR <0.018). PALM analysis showed significant group differences in regional deviations including the parahippocampal gyrus/amygdala, fusiform gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and cuneus for negative faces only, indicating that on average cases exhibit more age-related activation deviations in these regions. No significant differences emerged for negative deviations or anatomical measures. Deviations from positive/neutral face processing were significantly associated with aggression (ρ=0.24, pFDR=0.036). Linked ICA integrating deviations across all modalities yielded 20 components that together predicted 23% of the variance in DBD (McFadden's R²=23%; χ²=39.2, df=20, p=0.006). Component 8, strongly reflective of the default mode network (DMN) with high weightings in precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex, plus additional weightings in ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens, caudate), amygdala/hippocampus, and temporal gyrus, was significantly associated with the aggression factor across the whole sample (ρ=-0.28, pFDR=0.02; p=0.003 when outliers excluded). This component loaded most strongly on positive/neutral faces and shape processing with negligible anatomical loading, explaining 9% of variance in the aggression factor. Two components differed between cases and controls at nominal level (component 5: p=0.04; component 8: p=0.01) but did not survive FDR correction. The linked ICA model based on deviation scores showed superior fit compared to models using raw unmodeled contrast maps and JDs (AIC=173.9 vs 182.6; BIC=233.6 vs 248.0).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: 1) Small sample size limited normative modeling precision and prevented training TD-only reference models for the intersection dataset. 2) Cross-sectional design limits interpretation of age-related deviations as maturational delays; longitudinal studies are needed to validate developmental trajectories. 3) Insufficient power to statistically test sex differences in normative models. 4) Emotion matching task combined neutral and positive faces, potentially diluting subtle effects; future studies should separate positive face processing. 5) Inclusion of participants based on CBCL clinical aggression scores (n=25) increased DBD group heterogeneity, which is a limitation for case-control comparisons but supports individual-based normative modeling. 6) The normative model included both TD and DBD cases due to sample size constraints, with DBD frequency higher than in control populations; however, sensitivity analysis with larger anatomical dataset showed similar results using TD-only reference.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This study demonstrates the utility of combining normative modeling with multimodal data integration. The authors used GPR with 10-fold cross-validation for out-of-sample predictions, ComBat harmonization for scanner effects, and linked ICA on unthresholded deviation maps to integrate functional and structural information. The approach moved beyond traditional case-control comparisons to characterize widespread individual-level heterogeneity in DBD. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that deviation-based linked ICA outperformed raw-data linked ICA in predicting DBD and associating with aggression, supporting the value of normative modeling for placing individuals in a common reference framework before multimodal integration.

general_notes.general_notes: The study recruited participants from 9 European sites but retained only 5 sites for final fMRI analysis (Nijmegen, Mannheim, London, Barcelona, Madrid) to ensure minimum of 5 cases and 5 controls per site. Of the 77 DBD cases, 20 (25.97%) had comorbid ADHD diagnoses. Medication use was high in cases (66.23%): stimulants 39%, antipsychotics 20%, antidepressants 2.6%, other 2.6%. Cases and controls did not differ in movement during scanning (translation: p=.24; rotation: p=.11) or task performance. No site-by-group effects were found for demographics or clinical variables (Supplementary Table S5). The normative model predicted decreases in amygdala activity with age during negative face processing in the right amygdala; positive deviations in DBD may suggest maturational delay, though this interpretation requires longitudinal validation. Jacobian determinants were chosen as anatomical features because they quantify overall tissue expansion/contraction required to match each image to the population template, containing all information necessary to warp subject to template without arbitrary white/grey matter distinction. Full list of datasets available in supplement. The study references prior work using normative modeling in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder (Wolfers et al., 2018), and autism (Bethlehem et al., 2020; Floris et al., 2021; Zabihi et al., 2019).
